passage: Zubin, you said "whatever" about your spelling test. I know that word. When I was nine, in Jabalpur, I had a teacher who shouted at every wrong sum. "Ritu, wrong again!" I'd try, get it wrong, get shouted at. Try harder, still wrong, still shouted at. One day I simply stopped. When she asked for my answer I said "I don't know" before even reading the question. Why try, if trying and not trying ended the same way? It felt almost clever, like I'd found a way to hurt less. It took a different teacher, two years later, praising one right step at a time, before I believed my effort could change anything. So when you say whatever, beta, I don't hear lazy. I hear tired of losing.

qa.q: What would the teacher shout when young Ritu got a sum wrong?
qa.a: "Ritu, wrong again!"

qa.q: Why did not trying feel almost clever to young Ritu?
qa.a: Trying and not trying ended the same way, with shouting, so giving up seemed a sensible way to hurt less.

qa.q: What turning point helped Ritu start trying again?
qa.a: A new teacher two years later who praised one right step at a time, which showed that effort could make a difference.

qa.q: How might Zubin feel hearing "I don't hear lazy"?
qa.a: Zubin may feel understood rather than scolded, and more willing to talk about why the spelling test feels pointless.

grounding: An elder recalls giving up on maths at nine when effort never changed the outcome, making passivity feel sensible.

passage: Dilnaz had one old bicycle, her brother's, too tall for her, and only the narrow lane behind the flats to practise in, between parked scooters. Every evening for two weeks she tried. Every evening she wobbled, scraped a knee or bumped a scooter, and the watchman shouted. Her cousins laughed from the balcony. On Saturday Maria from the next building came down with her own small bike. "Want to try mine? It's lower." Dilnaz didn't even look up from the step. "Whatever. I can't ride. I'll never ride." "You haven't tried this one." "Doesn't matter. I always fall." Maria sat beside her, turning a pedal with her hand. Dilnaz picked at the scab on her knee and stared at the gutter.

qa.q: Where did Dilnaz practise riding?
qa.a: In the narrow lane behind the flats, between parked scooters.

qa.q: Why did Dilnaz refuse Maria's lower bike without even looking up?
qa.a: After two weeks of falling, shouting and laughter, she had come to believe nothing she did would work, so trying again felt pointless.

qa.q: What small choice could help Dilnaz try again?
qa.a: Trying Maria's lower bike for just one push somewhere quieter, so she has a real chance of success that proves effort can work.

qa.q: How might Maria feel sitting beside Dilnaz?
qa.a: Maria probably wants to help and may feel a little hurt by the "whatever", but sitting close shows she hasn't given up on Dilnaz.

grounding: A child who kept failing on a too-tall bike in a cramped lane stops trying and says 'whatever'.

passage: In the Lajpat Nagar flat, Simran's English notebook was mostly red. Every essay came back with "careless!" across the top, however long she spent on it. In August she rewrote one three times; it still came back red. So in September she stopped. When her Rekha masi, visiting from Jaipur, asked about the new essay, Simran shrugged. "Whatever. It'll be wrong anyway." She had written two lines and drawn a cat. "Did you even try?" Rekha asked. "Why would I? Trying and not trying get the same marks." Simran said it calmly, as if explaining the weather. Rekha looked through the old essays, saw how neat the rewritten one was, and felt her throat tighten.

qa.q: How many times did Simran rewrite the August essay?
qa.a: Three times; it still came back red.

qa.q: Why does Simran say it so calmly, as if explaining the weather?
qa.a: To her it is a plain fact that effort changes nothing, so giving up feels sensible rather than upsetting.

qa.q: What could Rekha masi do next to help Simran?
qa.a: Point to one specific thing that improved in the neat rewrite, and help her talk to the teacher about what "careless" means, so effort can be linked to results.

qa.q: What does Rekha feel when she sees the rewritten essay?
qa.a: Her throat tightens as she realises Simran worked hard and was still marked down, so the "whatever" hides disappointment, not laziness.

grounding: A child whose repeated effort keeps getting the same red marks stops trying and says it won't matter.

passage:
"Manoj, nets tomorrow? I'll bowl with you."
"Whatever, bhaiya."
Siddharth lowered his phone. "Whatever? You used to beg me."
"What's the point?" Manoj kept his eyes on the TV. "Every time I bowl, Coach says no-ball. I tried a shorter run-up. No-ball. I tried starting further back. No-ball. He shouts, and the whole team laughs."
"So you've stopped?"
"I'm just bad. Doesn't matter what I do."
Siddharth came and sat beside him. "Last Sunday you bowled four good ones to me in the lane."
"That's the lane. That's different."
"Maybe. Or maybe we mark your stride with chalk and sort out the no-ball together. Just ten balls."
Manoj shrugged. "You'll see. Same thing will happen."
But he didn't say no.

qa.q: What does Coach keep saying when Manoj bowls?
qa.a: Coach says no-ball.

qa.q: Why does 'Whatever' feel like the sensible answer to Manoj?
qa.a: He changed his run-up twice and still got no-ball and laughter; when effort seems to change nothing, not trying at least spares him more shame.

qa.q: What choice does Siddharth make, and why might it help?
qa.a: Instead of arguing, he recalls the four good balls and offers a small shared fix, chalk marks and just ten balls, a chance for effort to visibly work.

qa.q: How does Siddharth seem to feel hearing 'Whatever'?
qa.a: Siddharth seems surprised and concerned, since Manoj used to beg to play, and cares enough to put down his phone and sit beside him.

grounding: A child whose bowling keeps getting called and laughed at, whatever he changes, stops trying and says whatever.

passage: When I was nine, my Hemant Mama checked my maths homework every night after his shop closed. I'm Raghav. Every mistake got a sharp tap on the page and "Careless again!" I tried going slower. Still careless. I tried checking twice. Still wrong somewhere, still "careless". After a few months I stopped trying to get them right. I'd write any number and wait for the tap. When Amma asked why I'd gone so quiet, I said, "Whatever I do, it's wrong." It felt true. I'm eleven now, and Amma found me a tuition teacher who marks what I got right first. Last week I got four out of six, and I actually wanted to know what went wrong in the other two. That felt strange.

qa.q: What did Hemant Mama say at every mistake?
qa.a: 'Careless again!'

qa.q: Why did writing any number feel reasonable to Raghav at nine?
qa.a: Going slower and checking twice still brought the same tap and 'careless', so effort seemed useless and guessing at least cost less.

qa.q: What changed for Raghav, and why did it help?
qa.a: A tuition teacher who marks what Raghav got right first; seeing four out of six correct showed that effort counts, so Raghav wanted to fix the rest.

qa.q: What might Amma have noticed that led her to find a new teacher?
qa.a: Amma saw Raghav go quiet and heard 'Whatever I do, it's wrong', and seems to have understood the problem was the constant criticism, not laziness.

grounding: A child criticised for every mistake whatever the effort stops trying, until a different teacher shows that effort counts.

passage:
Class 4 note, Monday

Ujjwal used to put up his hand in maths. This term, he has stopped. Today, when I gave the fractions sheet, he wrote "whatever" at the top and put his head down. When I asked why, he said, "I get it wrong anyway. Even when I try, sir, you say it's wrong." I realised he has had three red-pen sheets in a row, and he was also scolded at home for his marks.

I sat with him and gave him one sum only, halves of a chapati, drawn on the board. He got it right. He looked at me as if he didn't believe it. I gave him a second. Right again. I'll start each class this week with one sum I'm sure he can do.

— Akash

qa.q: What did Ujjwal write at the top of the fractions sheet?
qa.a: "whatever"

qa.q: Why does writing 'whatever' feel sensible to Ujjwal?
qa.a: Ujjwal feels discouraged and hopeless, because even when he tries, the result is wrong, so trying seems pointless.

qa.q: What does Akash's plan of one easy sum aim to change?
qa.a: It gives Ujjwal small proofs that his effort works, which can slowly rebuild his belief that trying matters.

qa.q: How might Akash feel when Ujjwal looks surprised at getting the sum right?
qa.a: Akash likely feels moved and a bit hopeful, seeing that one success started to crack Ujjwal's belief that he always fails.

grounding: It shows, through a teacher's note, a child who stops trying and says whatever after repeated failure and scolding, because effort seems to change nothing.

passage:
Dear Diary,

Pradeep sir returned the handwriting books today. Mine had red lines again. "Messy, Deepika." I tried SO hard this time. I used the good pencil. I went slow. Still messy.

Last week I wrote fast and it was messy. This week slow, and messy. What's the point?

In the afternoon, when he gave the next page, I just did it any old way. Scribble scribble. My friend asked why and I said, whatever. Honestly it felt better than trying and getting red lines anyway.

At home Mummy asked about school. I said nothing happened.

I don't think my hand can be neat. Some people's hands just can't.

Deepika

qa.q: What did Deepika use to write carefully this time?
qa.a: The good pencil.

qa.q: Why did scribbling feel better to Deepika than trying?
qa.a: Deepika felt hurt and hopeless after red lines no matter what, so not trying felt safer and less disappointing.

qa.q: How could Pradeep sir help Deepika start trying again?
qa.a: He could point out one letter that improved and give a very small goal, so Deepika can see effort making a difference.

qa.q: How might Mummy feel if she knew what happened at school?
qa.a: Mummy might feel worried and sad that Deepika has given up and is hiding it, and would want to help.

grounding: It shows a child who, after being told the work was messy no matter what the effort, stops trying and says whatever.

passage: In their village near Jorhat, Bhupen wanted to ride the big bicycle like the other boys. Every evening he wheeled it to the mud road. Every evening he fell. His uncle watched from the shop and shouted, "Useless! You'll break it!" After two weeks, Bhupen stopped going to the road. When his sister Swati asked him to come, he shrugged. "Whatever. I can't ride." He sat on the steps and threw pebbles at the drain. One day the bicycle was leaning by the gate, the road empty, and Swati said, "I'll hold the seat." He shook his head and didn't look at it. The other boys raced past, ringing their bells.

qa.q: Where did Bhupen try to ride the bicycle?
qa.a: On the mud road.

qa.q: Why does staying on the steps feel sensible to Bhupen?
qa.a: After falling every evening and being shouted at, he feels defeated and ashamed, so trying seems pointless and not trying feels safer.

qa.q: What small step could help Bhupen try again?
qa.a: Swati holding the seat on an empty road, with no one shouting, could give him a tiny success to build on.

qa.q: How might Swati feel when Bhupen shakes his head?
qa.a: Swati may feel sad and a bit helpless, wanting to help her brother but seeing he's given up.

grounding: It shows a child who, after repeated falls and scolding, stops trying and says whatever, because effort seems to change nothing.

passage:
In Buenos Aires, Valentina, nine, had failed her times-tables quiz four weeks in a row. Every time, the teacher read the marks aloud. Every time, her mother sighed at home.
This week she didn't even look at the practice sheet. When her friend Mei offered to quiz her on the bus, Valentina shrugged. “Whatever. It doesn't matter what I do. I always get it wrong.”
“You got seven right last time.”
“And eight wrong.”
In the quiz, Valentina wrote a few answers, then put her pencil down and looked out of the window for the rest of the time.
Mei watched her. Valentina didn't look sad, exactly. She looked like she'd stopped expecting anything.

qa.q: How many weeks in a row had Valentina failed her times-tables quiz?
qa.a: She had failed it four weeks in a row.

qa.q: Why did Valentina put her pencil down in the quiz?
qa.a: After repeated failure and scolding she felt hopeless, believing effort changes nothing, so giving up felt sensible.

qa.q: How could an adult help Valentina start trying again?
qa.a: Give her very small, winnable practice and notice each success privately, so she sees that effort can change things.

qa.q: How does Mei see Valentina during the quiz?
qa.a: Mei sees a friend who has stopped expecting anything, and seems worried for her.

grounding: The passage shows a child who keeps failing and being sighed at no longer trying and saying “whatever,” as passivity comes to feel sensible.

passage:
At the boarding school in Darjeeling, the Class 5 English teacher had corrected Dolma's handwriting in red every single day since March. “Messy.” “Redo.” “Again.”
By August, Dolma had stopped trying to write neatly. She scribbled, handed it in, and stared at her desk while the red marks came back.
Her classmate Nilesh leaned over. “Why don't you write slowly? Then she won't complain.”
“I did, for months. She still wrote ‘messy.’” Dolma shrugged. “Whatever I do, it's wrong. So why bother?”
When the teacher asked her to copy the poem again, Dolma didn't argue. She didn't try either. She simply wrote the first line and stopped.
Nilesh looked at her page, then at her face. She looked tired in a way that didn't fit a ten-year-old.

qa.q: What did the teacher write on Dolma's work?
qa.a: “Messy,” “Redo” and “Again,” in red, every day since March.

qa.q: Why did Dolma stop trying to write neatly?
qa.a: She felt defeated and hopeless because nothing she did changed the red marks, so trying seemed pointless.

qa.q: What could the teacher change to help Dolma?
qa.a: Notice and name one improvement at a time instead of only “messy,” so Dolma can see that effort makes a difference.

qa.q: How does Nilesh experience watching Dolma give up?
qa.a: Nilesh seems worried and puzzled, noticing she looks tired in a way that doesn't fit a ten-year-old.

grounding: The passage shows a child whose efforts never changed a teacher's criticism stopping trying, because passivity feels sensible.

passage:
Week 1: Mahima, eleven, practised her Bharatanatyam steps every evening. Her dance teacher still said, “Wrong. Again,” in front of everyone, and her father Raghav said, “Why can't you get it right?”
Week 3: Mahima still went to class, but she stopped practising at home. When Raghav asked why, she said, “Doesn't matter. I'll get it wrong anyway.”
Week 6: In class, when the teacher called her forward, Mahima stood still and did the steps half-heartedly. She didn't care anymore, or looked like she didn't.
That evening, Raghav found her dance bells pushed under the bed. He sat down slowly. For the first time, he wondered if his own sighs had helped put them there. He picked them up and said, “Show me one step you like. Just one.”

qa.q: Where did Raghav find Mahima's dance bells?
qa.a: He found them pushed under the bed.

qa.q: Why did Mahima stop practising at home?
qa.a: After weeks of criticism no matter how hard she tried, she felt defeated and believed practice made no difference.

qa.q: What small step did Raghav take, and why could it help?
qa.a: He asked her to show one step she likes, a small, safe success that might rebuild her belief that effort matters.

qa.q: How does Raghav see his own part in Mahima's giving up?
qa.a: Raghav begins to feel regretful, wondering if his sighs helped push the bells under the bed.

grounding: The three beats show a child who is criticised no matter what she does stopping trying, and a parent beginning to see why.

passage:
"Abhinav, you've said 'whatever' three times today. Come, sit with your Ira Dadi. It was the winter I was eight, with fog so thick we couldn't see the gate.
Every evening my father made me practise handwriting on a slate. I tried round letters, he said too round. I tried thin letters, he said too thin. I wrote slowly, he said lazy. I wrote fast, he said careless. I cried, I tried again, and nothing I did was ever right.
By January, I stopped trying. I'd scratch any shape and hand it to him. When he asked why, I said, 'Whatever I do, it's wrong anyway.' And honestly, it felt sensible. Why work hard if the answer is always no?
It took a new teacher, who praised one good 'a' of mine, to show me effort could change something."

qa.q: What did young Ira practise every evening?
qa.a: She practised handwriting on a slate.

qa.q: Why did young Ira stop trying by January?
qa.a: She felt defeated and hopeless, because every kind of effort was called wrong, so giving up seemed sensible.

qa.q: What was the turning point in Ira Dadi's story?
qa.a: A new teacher praised one good 'a', which showed her that effort could actually change something.

qa.q: How might Ira's father have seen her scratching any shape?
qa.a: He may have thought she was being careless or stubborn, not realising his constant criticism had convinced her that trying was pointless.

grounding: It shows, through an elder's memory, a child who was criticised no matter what she did stopping trying, as passivity felt sensible when effort seemed to change nothing.

passage:
The Holi holidays were supposed to be for fun, but Yamini's tuition teacher, Madhuri ma'am, had given her the times tables from twelve to fifteen to learn before school reopened. And the power kept going off in the afternoons, so they worked on the steps in the heat.
Yamini had failed the tables test three times. Each time, her marks were read out in front of the class. Each time, she had practised harder.
Now Madhuri ma'am asked, "Thirteen sevens?"
Yamini didn't even think. "Whatever."
"Yamini, try."
"What for? I'll get it wrong anyway." She picked at a thread on her frock, staring at the gulal stains on the next house's wall. "Three times I learned it, and three times I failed."
Madhuri ma'am put the book down. For the first time, she didn't ask again.

qa.q: How many times had Yamini failed the tables test?
qa.a: She had failed it three times.

qa.q: Why does Yamini answer "Whatever" without even thinking?
qa.a: She feels defeated and hopeless; she practised harder each time and still failed, so trying again seems pointless to her.

qa.q: What small step could Madhuri ma'am take to help Yamini try again?
qa.a: She could start with just one table Yamini can already manage, praising each correct answer, so Yamini sees that her effort can change the result.

qa.q: How might Madhuri ma'am feel when she puts the book down?
qa.a: She may feel worried and a bit shaken, realising that more drilling won't work until Yamini believes trying can make a difference.

grounding: It shows a child who kept failing despite practice stopping trying and saying whatever, because effort seemed to change nothing.

passage:
On Diwali morning, the courtyard of the Lajpat Nagar flat was swept and ready for rangoli. Neelam, nine, knelt with the colour bowls.
"Not like that," said her father Ramesh. "The petals are uneven."
She started again. "Too much red."
Again. "The circle is crooked."
On the fourth try, when he said, "Neelam, the lines should be thinner," she put the bowl down and wiped her hands on her kurta.
"You do it."
"I'm teaching you."
"Whatever. It'll be wrong anyway." She went and sat on the steps, chin on her knees, watching the neighbours' children pour colours carelessly and laugh.
Ramesh looked at the four half-finished rangolis on the floor. For the first time that morning, he noticed there was nothing much wrong with any of them.

qa.q: How many times did Neelam start the rangoli?
qa.a: She started it four times.

qa.q: Why does Neelam say "Whatever. It'll be wrong anyway"?
qa.a: She feels discouraged and defeated, because every try was corrected, so giving up seems more sensible than trying again.

qa.q: What could Ramesh do now to help Neelam want to try again?
qa.a: He could praise something real in one of her rangolis and let her finish one her own way, so she sees her effort can succeed.

qa.q: How does Ramesh feel when he looks at the four rangolis?
qa.a: He seems to feel a pang of regret, noticing there was nothing much wrong with any of them.

grounding: It shows a child corrected at every attempt stopping trying and saying whatever, because effort seems to change nothing.

passage:
"Harsha, come, the kite's ready. Let's try again."
"Whatever."
"Whatever? It's Lohri tomorrow! Everyone's flying."
"I'll just crash it. I always crash it."
"You crashed it three times yesterday. That's how—"
"And Papa shouted every time. 'Pull, Harsha! Not like that! Why can't you do anything right?' I pull, it crashes. I don't pull, it crashes. Doesn't matter what I do."
"...He shouted that?"
"Every time. So I'll just watch."
"Okay. What if it's only you and me on the back roof? No shouting. I'll hold the string with you, and we just get it up. Just up."
"...It'll still crash."
"Maybe. Then we'll find out why. Come."
Gurpreet held out the spool and waited.

qa.q: How many times did Harsha crash the kite yesterday?
qa.a: Three times.

qa.q: Why does Harsha say "Whatever"?
qa.a: After being shouted at no matter what, Harsha feels defeated and hopeless; pulling or not, it crashes, so giving up seems the only sensible thing.

qa.q: What makes Gurpreet's offer a good next step?
qa.a: No shouting, holding the string together, and a tiny goal of "just up" give Harsha a chance to see that effort can change what happens.

qa.q: How might Gurpreet feel hearing what Papa said?
qa.a: Gurpreet seems taken aback and concerned, and wants to give Harsha a gentler, safer try.

grounding: A child who has been shouted at and keeps failing with a kite stops trying and says whatever, since effort seems to change nothing.
